'''Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat''' ({{IPA|fr|ivɔn ʃɔkɛ bʁy.a|lang|fr-Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat.wav}}; 29 December 1923 – 11 February 2025)<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Larousserie |first=David |date=12 February 2025 |title=La mort d'Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat, pionnière des études sur les ondes gravitationnelles |trans-title=Death of Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat, pioneer in the study of gravitational waves |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/disparitions/article/2025/02/12/la-mort-d-yvonne-choquet-bruhat-pionniere-des-etudes-sur-les-ondes-gravitationnelles_6543990_3382.html |access-date=20 February 2026 |work=Le Monde |language=French}}</ref> was a French mathematical physicist now best remembered for her investigation of the mathematics of [[general relativity]].<ref name=":0" /> Her proof that the [[Einstein field equations]] can be expressed as a [[Well-posed problem|well-posed]] [[initial value problem|initial-value problem]] was listed by the journal ''[[Classical and Quantum Gravity]]'' as one of thirteen "milestone" results in general relativity in an issue published in the centennial anniversary of its birth in 2015.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Will |first=Clifford |author-link=Clifford Martin Will |date=2015 |title=Focus issue: Milestones of general relativity |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/journal/0264-9381/page/Focus%20issue%20on%20Milestones%20of%20general%20relativity |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=32 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/32/12/120201 }}</ref> She also studied [[Non-abelian gauge transformation|non-Abelian gauge theory]], relativistic hydrodynamics, and [[supergravity]].<ref name=":1" />

Choquet-Bruhat was the first woman to be elected to the [[French Academy of Sciences]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Fechete |first=Iona |date=2016 |title=Accomplishments of Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat: The first woman member of the French Academy of Sciences |url=https://comptes-rendus.academie-sciences.fr/chimie/articles/10.1016/j.crci.2016.09.005/ |journal=Comptes Rendus Chimie |volume=19 |issue=11–12 |pages=1382–1387 |doi=10.1016/j.crci.2016.09.005|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref> and was a Grand Officer of the [[Legion of Honour]].<ref>{{in lang|fr}} [http://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichTexte.do;jsessionid=CC7375A5388FE26A3967D854AC88F767.tpdjo08v_3?cidTexte=JORFTEXT000019160499&dateTexte=&oldAction=rechJO Décret] of 11 July 2008, published in the [[Journal officiel de la République française|JO]] of 13 July 2008</ref>

==Early life and education==
Yvonne Bruhat was born in [[Lille]] on 29 December 1923<ref>{{Cite web |date=16 November 2007 |title=Madame Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat |url=http://www.ihes.fr/IHES/Scientifique/Seminaires/CvcHOQUET.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130703180622/http://web.archive.org/web/20071116100358/http://www.ihes.fr/IHES/Scientifique/Seminaires/CvcHOQUET.html |archive-date=3 July 2013 |access-date=28 January 2026 |website=French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS)}}</ref> in an intellectual family.<ref name=":0" /> Her mother was philosophy professor Berthe Hubert and her father was physicist [[Georges Bruhat]],<ref name=":1" /> who died in 1945 in the [[Sachsenhausen concentration camp]].<ref name=":0" /> He was sent there after refusing to divulge information on the [[French Resistance]] to Nazi occupation.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Dafermos |first=Mihalis |author-link=Mihalis Dafermos |date=4 June 2025 |title=Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat obituary: mathematician who established that Einstein's equations mirror the real world |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-01763-z |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=642 |issue=8067 |pages=298 |doi=10.1038/D41586-025-01763-Z|bibcode=2025Natur.642..298D |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Her brother [[François Bruhat]] also became a mathematician.<ref name=":1" />

Bruhat attended secondary school in Paris, earning her [[Baccalauréat]] in 1941, at the top of her class.<ref name=":2" /> She received the silver medal for physics in the prestigious [[Concours général|Concours Général]] national competition.<ref name=":1" /> In her view, mathematics and the natural sciences were the best ways to understand the Universe.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Bieri |first=Lydia |date=March 2020 |title=Book Review: ''A Lady Mathematician in this Strange Universe: Memoirs'' |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=67 |issue=3 |pages=384–9 |doi=10.1090/noti2055 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Uncertain whether to study medicine, physics, or mathematics, she decided on the last.<ref name=":0" /> She wanted to research rather than teach, as was more usual for women at the time.<ref name=":0" /> From 1943 to 1946 she studied at the [[École normale supérieure de jeunes filles]] (a [[Single-sex education|girls' school]], also known as the École normale de [[Sèvres]]) near Paris.<ref name=":1" />

==Career==
From 1946 to 1949, she was an assistant at the [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École normale supérieure]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1947, Bruhat undertook research under the supervision of mathematical physicist [[André Lichnerowicz]],<ref name=":0" /> who invited her to be his doctoral student after seeing her excellent marks on an examination for future high-school teachers.<ref name=":7" /> But unlike most mathematicians at the time, she did not want to follow the trend towards increasing [[Abstraction (mathematics)|abstraction]] and preferred to remain close to physics, motivated by her desire to better understand nature.<ref name=":0" /> [[Jean Leray]], an expert on the theory of [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]], suggested that she investigate whether or not the Einstein field equations of general relativity were well-posed.<ref name=":0" /> This became the topic of her dissertation,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fourès-Bruhat |first=Yvonne |date=1952 |title=Théorème d'existence pour certains systèmes d'équations aux dérivées partielles non linéaires |trans-title=Existence Theorem for Certain Systems of Non-Linear Partial Differential Equations |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/acta-mathematica/volume-88/issue-none/Th%c3%a9or%c3%a8me-dexistence-pour-certains-syst%c3%a8mes-d%c3%a9quations-aux-d%c3%a9riv%c3%a9es-partielles-non/10.1007/BF02392131.full |journal=[[Acta Mathematica]] |language=French |volume=88 |pages=141–225 |doi=10.1007/BF02392131 |bibcode=1952AcMa...88..141F }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> for which she earned her doctorate in 1951.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|103574}}</ref> While it was known that the equations of motion derived from [[Newton's laws of motion]] and [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|gravitation]] yielded unique solutions with initial conditions, whether this was true for Einstein's gravitational field equations remained unproven until her landmark thesis.<ref name=":0" /> 

Her work guaranteed the predictability of the universe as described by general relativity.<ref name=":0" /> Her work also lent credence to [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]], predicted by general relativity, but initially doubted by Einstein, who thought that they were merely a mathematical artefact of [[Coordinate system|coordinate]] choices.<ref name=":0" /> In two papers published in 1916 and 1918, Einstein had only shown that waves were solutions to the [[Linearized gravity|linearized gravitational field equations]]. Bruhat demonstrated that this was also true for the fully non-linear equations.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Bieri |first=Lydia |author-link=Lydia Bieri |date=24 January 2024 |title=From the Initial Value Problem for the Einstein Equations to Gravitational Waves |url=http://www.isgrg.org/YvonneChoquetBruhat100Bieri.pdf |publisher=International Society on General Relativity and Gravitation}}</ref> She expressed the Einstein field equations in vacuum using [[Harmonic coordinate condition|harmonic coordinates]], previously introduced by [[Théophile De Donder]] and [[Cornelius Lanczos]], in which case they become non-linear [[Hyperbolic partial differential equation|hyperbolic]] partial differential equations,<ref name=":7" /> and as such could describe the propagation of waves.<ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last1=Yau |first1=Shing-Tung |author-link1=Shing-Tung Yau |title=The Gravity of Math: How Geometry Rules the Universe |last2=Nadis |first2=Steve |publisher=Basic Books |year=2024 |isbn=978-1-541-60429-2}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=133-4}} While [[Georges Darmois]] had already tackled the problem for [[Analytic function|analytic]] solutions, Bruhat's proof applied to non-analytic cases as well.<ref name=":7" /> 

She also showed that gravitational waves could not propagate at an arbitrary speed; they must travel at the [[speed of light]] in vacuum.<ref name=":0" /> [[Causality (physics)|Causality]] was therefore not violated.<ref name=":7" /> With the 2017 detection of both gravitational and [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic waves]] from  [[GW170817]], the merger of two [[Neutron star|neutron stars]] in the galaxy [[NGC 4993]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Abbott |first=B. P. |display-authors=etal |date=October 2017 |title=Multi-messenger Observations of a Binary Neutron Star Merger |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters |volume=848 |issue=2 |at=L12 |arxiv=1710.05833 |bibcode=2017ApJ...848L..12A |doi=10.3847/2041-8213/aa91c9 |s2cid=217162243 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Bruhat's faith in her mathematical work was vindicated by [[multi-messenger astronomy]].<ref name=":0" /> 

With some help from Leray, Bruhat and her first husband, Léonce Fourès, were offered fellowships at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] (IAS) in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], in the academic year 1951–51.<ref name=":7" /> During her time there, she met a number of scientific luminaries, including the Institute director, [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]], former scientific director of the Manhattan Project,<ref name=":2" /> [[John Archibald Wheeler]], who became her friend,<ref name=":0" /> and [[John von Neumann]], who showed her an early electronic computer he built called the [[IAS machine]].<ref name=":7" /> She also met [[Albert Einstein]], father of general relativity, whom she remembered as a kind and friendly man.<ref name=":0" /> She presented her work to him on his [[blackboard]].<ref name=":0" /> She described this as a happy time in her life.<ref name=":7" /> After their time at the IAS, she and her husband accepted positions at the [[University of Marseille]].<ref name=":7" /> 

While a number of [[Solutions of the Einstein field equations|solutions to the Einstein field equations]] had already been obtained, her contributions to the mathematics of general relativity stimulated interest in the topic among mathematicians.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Isenberg |first=James |author-link=James A. Isenberg |date=2013 |title=A brief assessment of the work of Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat |url=http://www.ihes.fr/jsp/site/Portal.jsp?document_id=3390&portlet_id=1153 |access-date=20 February 2026 |publisher=Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150715180614/http://www.ihes.fr/jsp/site/Portal.jsp?document_id=3390&portlet_id=1153|archive-date=15 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Her dissertation showed that general relativity could be handled with mathematical [[Rigour#Mathematics|rigour]] and became the basis for future studies on the mathematics of general relativity.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|page=135}} In the long run, it also facilitated the development of [[numerical relativity]],<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" /> making it possible to run [[Computational physics|computer simulations]] of the [[Two-body problem in general relativity|motion of two bodies]] (such as black holes and other [[Compact object|compact objects]] in a [[binary system]]), their merger, and the gravitational waves they emit during the process.<ref name=":7" /> In 2005, [[Frans Pretorius]] successfully wrote the first computer simulation of two merging black holes based on Choquet-Bruhat's work, in particular, her use of harmonic coordinates.<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|pages=142–3}} Simulations of this kind were used in analysing the [[First observation of gravitational waves|first detection of gravitational waves]] in 2015.<ref name=":2" /> Along with other key figures such as Wheeler, [[Peter Bergmann]], and [[Dennis W. Sciama|Dennis Sciama]], her studies and collaborations spurred the revival and growth of research in general relativity during the second half of the 1950s.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lalli |first1=Roberto |title=The Renaissance of General Relativity in Context |last2=Howey |first2=Riaz |last3=Wintergrün |first3=Dirk |publisher=[[Birkhäuser]] |year=2020 |editor-last=Blum |editor-first=Alexander S. |series=Einstein Studies |volume=16 |chapter=The Socio-Epistemic Networks of General Relativity, 1925–1970 |pages=15–84 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-50754-1_2 |isbn=978-3-030-50753-4 |editor-last2=Lalli |editor-first2=Roberto |editor-last3=Renn |editor-first3=Jürgen |editor-link3=Jürgen Renn}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=48}} She attended the [[Chapel Hill Conference|Conference on the Role of Gravitation in Physics]] in [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina]], in 1957.<ref name=":7" /> This conference marked the beginning of the renaissance of general relativity after the Second World War.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Pais|first=Abraham|title=Subtle Is the Lord: The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein|title-link=Subtle is the Lord|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-192-80672-7|pages=|chapter=|orig-date=1982|author-link=Abraham Pais}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=270}} The [[International Society on General Relativity and Gravitation]] (ISGRG) was formed 14 years later.<ref name=":7" /> Bruhat served its president from 1980 to 1983.<ref name=":0" />  

In 1958, she was awarded the [[CNRS Silver Medal]].<ref name="UCLA">[http://www.physics.ucla.edu/~cwp/Phase2/Choquet-Bruhat,_Yvonne@922345678.html#honors Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat page] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120219231821/http://www.physics.ucla.edu/~cwp/Phase2/Choquet-Bruhat,_Yvonne@922345678.html#honors |date=February 19, 2012 }} at [http://www.physics.ucla.edu/~cwp/dev/exp.1.html ''Contribution of 20th Century Women to Physics'' pages] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029200133/http://www.physics.ucla.edu/~cwp/dev/exp.1.html |date=October 29, 2014 }} of [[UCLA]]</ref> From 1958 to 1959 she taught at the [[University of Reims]]. In 1960 relocated to [[Sorbonne (building)|the Sorbonne]] in Paris.<ref name=":7" /> When this was later reorganized, she moved to Paris VI (later the [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] or UPMC),<ref name=":7" /> and remained there until her retirement in 1990.<ref name=":7" /> Afterward, she occupied a position to the Institute for Higher Scientific Studies ([[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques|IHÉS]]).<ref name=":0" /> At the UPMC she continued to make significant contributions to mathematical physics, notably in general relativity, supergravity, and the non-Abelian [[Gauge theory|gauge theories]] of the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics.<ref name=":1" />  

During the 1950s and 1960s, she generalized the main result of her doctoral dissertation to cases of the Einstein field equations in the presence of various types of matter.<ref name=":5" /> In 1969 she and [[Robert Geroch]] introduced the notion of maximal Cauchy development,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Choquet-Bruhat |first1=Yvonne |last2=Geroch |first2=Robert |date=1969 |title=Global aspects of the Cauchy problem in general relativity |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01645389 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=329–335 |bibcode=1969CMaPh..14..329C |doi=10.1007/BF01645389 |s2cid=121522405 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> important in the study of global aspects of the [[Cauchy problem]] in general relativity and the [[Penrose–Hawking singularity theorems|theorems on gravitational singularities]] of [[Roger Penrose]] and [[Stephen Hawking]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1976, she and [[Jerrold E. Marsden|Jerrold Marsden]] proved the [[Positive mass theorem|positive-mass theorem]] for the case of a vacuum flat spacetime near [[Minkowski space|Minkowski]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Damour |first=Thibault |author-link=Thibault Damour |date=24 January 2024 |title=Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat: a Mathematician in Einstein's Universe |url=http://www.isgrg.org/GRGYCB100Damourv2.pdf |publisher=The International Society on General Relativity and Gravitation}}</ref> With [[Cécile DeWitt-Morette]] and Margaret Dillard-Bleick, she published monograph titled ''Analysis, Manifolds and Physics'', detailing the relevance of [[global analysis]] for physics.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=12 February 2025 |title=Décès de Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat |trans-title=Death of Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat |url=https://smf.emath.fr/actualites-smf/deces-de-yvonne-choquet-bruhat |access-date=20 February 2026 |publisher=[[Société mathématique de France]] |language=French}}</ref> Her work in 1981 with [[Demetrios Christodoulou]] demonstrated the existence of global solutions of the [[Yang–Mills equations|Yang–Mills]], [[Higgs field|Higgs]], and [[spinor field]] equations in 3+1 dimensions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Choquet-Bruhat |first1=Yvonne |last2=Christodoulou |first2=Demetrios |author-link2=Demetrios Christodoulou |date=1981 |title=Existence of global solutions of the Yang-Mills, Higgs and spinor field equations in 3 + 1 dimensions |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/?id=ASENS_1981_4_14_4_481_0 |journal=Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=481–506 |doi=10.24033/asens.1417}}</ref> In 1984 she examined results in supergravity that can be extended to 11 dimensions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Choquet-Bruhat |first=Yvonne |date=1985 |title=Causalité des théories de supergravité |url=https://www.numdam.org/book-part/AST_1985__S131__79_0/ |department=Astérisque |journal=Élie Cartan et les mathématiques d'aujourd'hui |issue=S131 |pages=79–93}}</ref>

In 1978 Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat was elected a correspondent to the Academy of Sciences and on 14 May 1979 became the first woman to be elected a full member.<ref name=":0" /> In 1985 she was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1986 she was chosen to deliver the prestigious [[Noether Lecture]] by the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]].<ref name=":1" /> In 2006, she delivered a talk titled "Results and Open Problems in [[Mathematics of general relativity|Mathematical General Relativity]]" at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Madrid.<ref name=":3" /> In 2011, she exhibited a simplified version of ([[Spinor|spinorial]]) proof of the positive-energy theorem by [[Edward Witten]], valid for any number of dimensions.<ref name=":6" /> She completed her last technical book, ''Introduction to General Relativity, Black Holes & Cosmology'', in 2014.<ref name=":3" />

== Technical research contributions ==
Choquet-Bruhat's best-known research deals with the mathematical nature of the initial data formulation of [[general relativity]]. A summary of results can be phrased purely in terms of standard [[differential geometry|differential geometric]] objects.
* An '''initial data set''' is a triplet {{math|(''M'', ''g'', ''k'')}} in which {{mvar|M}} is a three-dimensional [[smooth manifold]], {{mvar|g}} is a smooth Riemannian metric on {{mvar|M}}, and {{mvar|k}} is a smooth (0,2)-tensor field on {{mvar|M}}.
* Given an initial data set {{math|(''M'', ''g'', ''k'')}}, a '''development''' of {{math|(''M'', ''g'', ''k'')}} is a four-dimensional [[Lorentzian manifold]] {{math|({{overline|''M''}}, {{overline|''g''}})}} together with a smooth [[embedding]] {{math|''f'' : ''M'' → {{overline|''M''}}}} and a smooth unit normal vector field along {{mvar|f}} such that {{math|''f''<sup> *</sup>{{overline|''g''}} {{=}} ''g''}} and such that the [[second fundamental form]] of {{mvar|f}}, relative to the given normal vector field, is {{mvar|k}}.
In this sense, an initial data set can be viewed as the prescription of the submanifold geometry of an embedded spacelike hypersurface in a Lorentzian manifold.
* An initial data set {{math|(''M'', ''g'', ''k'')}} satisfies the '''vacuum constraint equations''', or is said to be a '''vacuum initial data set''', if the following two equations are satisfied:
::<math>\begin{align}
R_g-|k|_g^2+(\operatorname{tr}_gk)^2&=0\\
\operatorname{div}_gk-d(\operatorname{tr}_gk)&=0.
\end{align}</math>
: Here {{math|''R''<sub>''g''</sub>}} denotes the [[scalar curvature]] of {{mvar|g}}.
One of Choquet-Bruhat's seminal 1952 results states the following:
{{blockquote|Every vacuum initial data set {{math|(''M'', ''g'', ''k'')}} has a development {{math|''f'' : ''M'' → ({{overline|''M''}}, {{overline|''g''}})}} such that {{math|{{overline|''g''}}}} has zero [[Ricci curvature]], and such that every inextendible timelike curve in the Lorentzian manifold {{math|({{overline|''M''}}, {{overline|''g''}})}} intersects {{math|''f''(''M'')}} exactly once.}}
Briefly, this can be summarized as saying that there exists a [[Vacuum solution (general relativity)|vacuum spacetime]] {{math|({{overline|''M''}}, {{overline|''g''}})}} for which {{math|''f''(''M'')}} is a [[Cauchy surface]]. Such a development is called a '''globally hyperbolic vacuum development'''. Choquet-Bruhat also proved a uniqueness theorem:

{{blockquote|Given any two globally hyperbolic vacuum developments {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub> : ''M'' → ({{overline|''M''}}<sub>1</sub>, {{overline|''g''}}<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|''f''<sub>2</sub> : ''M'' → ({{overline|''M''}}<sub>2</sub>, {{overline|''g''}}<sub>2</sub>)}} of the same vacuum initial data set, there is an open subset {{math|''U''<sub>1</sub>}} of {{math|{{overline|''M''}}<sub>1</sub>}} containing {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>(''M'')}} and an open subset {{math|''U''<sub>2</sub>}} of {{math|{{overline|''M''}}<sub>2</sub>}} containing {{math|''f''<sub>2</sub>(''M'')}}, together with an isometry {{math|''i'' : (''U''<sub>1</sub>, {{overline|''g''}}<sub>1</sub>) → (''U''<sub>2</sub>, {{overline|''g''}}<sub>2</sub>)}} such that {{math|''i''(''f''<sub>1</sub>(''p'')) {{=}} ''f''<sub>2</sub>(''p'')}} for all {{mvar|p}} in {{mvar|M}}.}}

In a slightly imprecise form, this says: given any embedded spacelike hypersurface {{mvar|M}} of a Ricci-flat Lorentzian manifold {{math|{{overline|''M''}}}}, the geometry of {{math|{{overline|''M''}}}} near {{mvar|M}} is fully determined by the submanifold geometry of {{mvar|M}}.

In an article written with [[Robert Geroch]] in 1969, Choquet-Bruhat fully clarified the nature of uniqueness. With a two-page argument in [[point-set topology]] using [[Zorn's lemma]], they showed that Choquet-Bruhat's above existence and uniqueness theorems automatically imply a global uniqueness theorem:<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Choquet-Bruhat |first1=Yvonne |last2=Geroch |first2=Robert |date=December 1969 |title=Global aspects of the Cauchy problem in general relativity |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01645389 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=329–335 |doi=10.1007/BF01645389 |bibcode=1969CMaPh..14..329C |issn=0010-3616 |via=Research Gate|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
{{blockquote|Any vacuum initial data set {{math|(''M'', ''g'', ''k'')}} has a '''maximal globally hyperbolic vacuum development''', meaning a globally hyperbolic vacuum development {{math|''f'' : ''M'' → ({{overline|''M''}}, {{overline|''g''}})}} such that, for any other globally hyperbolic vacuum development {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub> : ''M'' → ({{overline|''M''}}<sub>1</sub>, {{overline|''g''}}<sub>1</sub>)}}, there is an open subset {{mvar|U}} of {{math|{{overline|''M''}}}} containing {{math|''f''(''M'')}} and an isometry {{math|''i'' : {{overline|''M''}}<sub>1</sub> → ''U''}} such that {{math|''i''(''f''<sub>1</sub>(''p'')) {{=}} ''f''(''p'')}} for all {{mvar|p}} in {{mvar|M}}.<br /><br />Any two maximal globally hyperbolic vacuum developments of the same vacuum initial data are isometric to one another.}}
It is now common to study such developments. For instance, the well-known theorem of [[Demetrios Christodoulou]] and [[Sergiu Klainerman]] on stability of Minkowski space asserts that if {{math|(ℝ<sup>3</sup>, ''g'', ''k'')}} is a vacuum initial data set with {{mvar|g}} and {{mvar|k}} sufficiently close to zero (in a certain precise form), then its maximal globally hyperbolic vacuum development is [[geodesically complete]] and geometrically close to [[Minkowski space]].

Choquet-Bruhat's proof makes use of a clever choice of coordinates, the [[Harmonic coordinate condition|wave coordinates]] (which are the Lorentzian equivalent to the [[harmonic coordinates]]), in which the Einstein equations become a system of [[hyperbolic partial differential equations]], for which well-posedness results can be applied.

==Personal life and death==
[[File:Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat 2.jpeg|thumb|Choquet-Bruhat in 2006]]

In 1947, she married fellow mathematician Léonce Fourès.<ref name=":7" /> Their daughter Michelle is an [[ecologist]]. Her doctoral work and early research was under the name Yvonne Fourès-Bruhat.<ref name=":2" /> In 1960, Bruhat and Fourès divorced.<ref name=":7" /> 

The following year she married the mathematician [[Gustave Choquet]]<ref name=":7" /> and [[Maiden and married names|changed her last name]] to Choquet-Bruhat. She and Choquet had two children: a son, neuroscientist [[Daniel Choquet|Daniel]], and a daughter, medical doctor Geneviève.

Her memoir, from her academic and personal life, was translated into English in 2018.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gray |first=Mary W. |author-link=Mary W. Gray |date=2018 |title=Review: ''A Lady Mathematician in This Strange Universe: Memoirs'' |journal=[[Mathematical Intelligencer]] |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=86–8 |doi=10.1007/s00283-018-9810-x }}</ref>

Choquet-Bruhat died on 11 February 2025 in Merignac, France (33700), at the age of 101.<ref>{{Cite web |date=11 February 2025 |title=Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat (1923–2025) |url=https://www.ihes.fr/yvonne-choquet-bruhat/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20260129043620/https://www.ihes.fr/yvonne-choquet-bruhat/ |archive-date=29 January 2026 |access-date=29 January 2026 |website=IHES |language=fr-FR}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

==Honours and awards==
* Médaille d'Argent du Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, 1958
* Prix Henri de Parville of the Académie des Sciences, 1963
* Member (since 1965), {{lang | fr | Comite International de Relativite Generale et Gravitation}} (President 1980–1983)<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20170323203623/http://www.awm-math.org/noetherbrochure/Choquet86.html Presentation on the site for the Association for Women in Mathematics]</ref>
* Member, Académie des Sciences, Paris (elected 1979)
* Elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1985
* Association for Women in Mathematics Noether Lecturer, 1986
* Commandeur de la Légion d'honneur, 1997
* [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]], 2003
* She was elevated to the 'Grand Officier' and 'Grand Croix' dignities in the Légion d'Honneur in 2008.<ref>{{MacTutor|title=Yvonne Suzanne Marie-Louise Choquet-Bruhat|id=Choquet-Bruhat}}</ref>

In 2026, Choquet-Bruhat was announced as one of 72 historical women in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] whose names are proposed to be added to the [[List of the 72 names on the Eiffel Tower|72 men]] already celebrated on the [[Eiffel Tower]]. [[Anne Hidalgo]], the Mayor of Paris, announced this on the recommendation of a committee led by [[Isabelle Vauglin]] of [[Femmes et Sciences]] and Jean-François Martins, which represents the operating company that manages the Eiffel Tower.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eiffel Tower: a list of 72 women scientists will soon be inscribed on the Parisian monument |url=https://www.sortiraparis.com/en/news/in-paris/articles/340564-eiffel-tower-list-of-72-women-scientists-soon-to-be-honored-on-the-paris-landmark |access-date=20 February 2026 |website=Sortira Paris |language=en|date=27 January 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=26 January 2026 |title=Eiffel Tower to honor 72 women scientists for posterity |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/france/article/2026/01/26/eiffel-tower-to-honor-72-women-in-science-for-posterity_6749828_7.html |access-date=20 February 2026 |language=en|last=Jacquin|first=Jean-Baptiste|archive-url=|archive-date=|work=[[Le Monde]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Les noms des 72 femmes pour la Tour Eiffel ont été révélés. |url=https://www.femmesetsciences.fr/news/les-noms-des-72-femmes-pour-la-tour-eiffel-ont-%C3%A9t%C3%A9-r%C3%A9v%C3%A9l%C3%A9 |access-date=2026-06-26 |website=Femmes & Sciences |language=fr }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://10ca8303-b3dc-4a91-9dcc-2d2b91792b47.usrfiles.com/ugd/10ca83_3838bd19a41a4e83927cfc8fe0f50404.pdf |title=72 femmes de sciences pour la tour Eiffel |trans-title=72 Women Scientists for the Eiffel Tower |work=Femmes & Sciences |language=fr |access-date=2026-06-26 }}</ref>
